title: AI agents: workflows, tools & guardrails
description: Build useful automation with clear boundaries and human control.
objectives: Distinguish fixed workflows from agent decisions
explanation: A workflow follows a defined sequence of steps. An agent lets a model choose some next steps based on observations. Use a fixed workflow when the route is predictable; add model-directed decisions only where flexibility creates measurable value. Every extra decision creates another opportunity for failure.

Tools expose actions or information through a defined interface. Treat a proposed call as an untrusted request: check arguments and permissions before execution. Separate read-only research from actions such as sending a message or changing a record. Require human approval where the consequence warrants it.

Memory can preserve useful state, but it can also preserve stale or sensitive information. Define what is stored, for how long, and who may access it. Add a step budget, timeout, and stop condition. Multi-agent patterns multiply communication and coordination costs, so first test whether one controlled workflow is sufficient.

terms.definition: An application capability exposed through an interface.
A rule that ends a workflow or agent loop.

example: A support agent can search articles, draft a reply, and present it to a human. Give search read-only permissions. Keep sending behind a separate approval step that displays the recipient and exact message. Stop after three unsuccessful searches.
mistakes: Assuming another agent independently verifies facts.
Keeping memory forever without a deletion policy.
exercise: Draw a support workflow with one model decision. Add an approval boundary, a maximum step count, and an escalation path.

questions.question: When is a fixed workflow a good choice?
questions.answer: When the sequence is predictable and testable, a fixed workflow can be simpler and easier to control than model-directed planning.
questions.distractor: Only when no language model is used anywhere.

questions.question: What should a send-message approval show?
questions.answer: The exact recipient, message, and relevant consequences so the person approves the concrete action.

questions.question: An agent keeps repeating failed searches. What prevents runaway cost?
questions.answer: Enforce step and time budgets, detect repeated failures, and escalate through a defined stop condition.
questions.distractor: Tell the agent to try forever.

questions.question: Does adding a second agent guarantee verification?
questions.answer: No. Agents can share assumptions or repeat errors; verification needs independent evidence and explicit checks.
questions.distractor: Yes, agreement between two agents proves truth.

questions.question: What policy should agent memory have?
questions.answer: Define purpose, access, retention, correction, and deletion so stored state remains useful and appropriately controlled.
questions.distractor: Store every interaction permanently by default.
